full_judgment:
2. The petitioners No. 1-17 instituted Partition suit No. 16 of 1973 in the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Satkania against the opposite party Nos. 1-3 and others. The plaint having been rejected by the trial court an appeal was taken to the District Judge and the appellate Court remanded the suit to the trial Court for amendment of the plaint. After the remand the defendants filed an objection to valuation of the suit and the value of the suit was determined at Tk. 2,700/-. As, against that order the revisional case No. 92 of 1979 was preferred to the Court of District Judge, Chittagong who allowed the revision case with the direction to re-assess the valuation of the suit on the basis of the documents. Subsequently, due to change of territorial jurisdiction of the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Satkania, the suit was transferred to the Court of Munsif, Bashkhali who received on 16.11.83 the record of the case. The date of hearing was notified in the notice Board. The suit on transfer was re-numbered as Partition Suit No. 560 of 1983. The learned Munsif after several adjournments of the hearing of the suit posted the same for peremptory hearing on 27.12.1983 and passed an ex-parte preliminary decree in absence of the opposite parties Nos. 1-3. A final decree was also passed and possession was delivered to the petitioners No. 1-24. Against the final decree Partition Appeal No. 407 of 1984 is pending before the Court of District Judge. 

 3. The opposite parties No. 1-3 before me filed Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 1984 on 29.5.1984 under Order 9 rule 13 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte preliminary decree of the Court of Munsif, Bashkhali alleging, interlaia, that they were not aware of the- transmission of the record of the suit after hearing the valuation matter by the appellant Court as the learned Advocate and his clerk did not inform about the transmission of the record from the court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Satkania and they were under bona fide belief that they would be informed about the hearing of the suit by the learned Advocate and his clerk. On 14.5.1984 when the petitioner NO.4 disclosed about the ex parte decree to the witnesses the opposite parties No. 1-3 filed Miscellaneous Case No.88 of 1984 on 16.5. 1984 having enquired about the suit and knowing about the ex parte decree. The petitioner Nos. 1-17 contested the ground of limitation and defect of parties. They further alleged that the ex parte decree was passed in presence of the opposite-parties Nos. 1-3 on 27.12.1983 and the case was filed to harass them. 

 4. The learned Munsif dismissed the Miscellaneous Case on contest holding that the opposite parties Nos. 1-3 were not prevented by sufficient cause the case was barred by limitation and for want of an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act for condo nation of delay. 

 5. The Miscellaneous Appeal No. 308 of 1985 of the opposite-parties against that order was allowed restoring the suit by the impugned order dated 27.9.1986 passed by the learned District Judge. 

 6. Mr. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioners first, urged that provisions of Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure are not attracted in the instant case inasmuch as there are specific provisions provided in the Code for the remedy and there being three alternative remedies available to the opposite-parties namely by way an application under Order 9, rule 13 for setting aside the ex parte decree, an appeal against the ex parte decree and an independent suit for declaration that the ex parte decree was bad and illegal the lower appellate court acted illegally in invoking the inherent jurisdiction under Section 151 of the Code in passing the impugned order. He further urged that the lower appellate court wrongly following the decision in the case of Master Abdul Aziz Vs. Abani Mohan Kukuherjee and others reported in 30 DLR (SC), 221 passed the impugned order. He referred me to the following observation of their Lordships. 

 "What has been held in the above cases is that the Court has an inherent power under Section 151 of the Code to set aside its order passed under a misapprehension of facts when true facts are brought to light and that the Court has also power under the aforesaid Section 151 of the Code to vacate an order obtained by misleading the Court and practicing fraud upon it." 

 7. He submitted that from the above observation it appears that there was misrepresentation in obtaining the order in that case but in the instant case no such misrepresentation or fraud was practiced upon the court by the petitioners in obtaining the ex parte decree. The submission seemingly seems to have force. Mr. Fazlul Karim, on the other hand, submitted that the petitioners did not disclose to the trial Court that an order was passed by the appellate Court regarding the re-assessment of the valuation of the suit and the petitioners upon such suppression obtained the ex parte decree. He further submitted that as no notice was given by the Court regarding transfer of the suit the ex parte decree was liable to be set aside. He placed reliance in support of his contention upon the case of Hiralal and others Vs. State and Bihar, 1968 Pat. 439. In that case 3 cases were pending before the District Judge, Arrah. The said cases subsequently were transferred to the court of Subordinate Judge for disposal. But the court did not notify the fact of transfer of the case to the parties or their pleaders. It was held that in cases of transfer made by the court Suo motu notice of transfer must be given to the parties or their lawyers. 

 8. In my opinion want of notice of transfer of the suit is a sufficient ground for the opposite parties Nos. 1-3 in this case for not appearing at the time when the suit was called on for hearing by the learned Munsif, In the case of Ram Sukul Pathak Vs. Kesho Prashand Singh 1918 Pat., 341, it was held by the learned Chief Justice who delivered the judgment of the report that; 

 "It seems to me that it would be desirable in these cases where an order of transfer is made that notice should be given in every case to the parties or their representatives. I find a passage in the judgment of J wale Prasad. J., which deals with this point and with which I entirely agree. He says: 

 "In my mind such an important order as the transfer of a case from one court to another should invariably be communicated to the persons concerned and in token of such communication the signature of the parties or their pleaders should be obtained and when the signatures are not obtained the order-sheet should show that the information has been communicated". 

 9. From the facts of this case before one it appears that there was order by the appellate court on remand to reassess the valuation of the suit by the trial Court on the basis of the documents already put in the trial Court and it was within knowledge of the petitioners as they were present in the trial Court when the ex parte decree was passed and as such it was their duty to bring to the knowledge of the Court that the suit was not valued in terms of the remand order of the lower appellate court. Withholding of such material fact from the knowledge of Court was deliberate and willful omission on the part of the petitioners and, in my opinion, such act tantamount to practising fraud upon the court in obtaining an ex parte decree in this case. The petitioners did conceal this from the trial Court at the time when the ex-part decree was made in order to obtain advantage of ex parte decree. Had they brought this fact to notice of the court it certainly ought not to have made the ex parte decree rather it would have proceeded to reasses the valuation in accordance with the direction of the court of appeal. The contention of the learned Advocate that the lower appellate court wrongly applied the principle of law enunciated in the case of A. Aziz is not tenable. It is true, when alternative remedy is provided in the Code a party is not entitled to invoke the provisions of section 151 of the Code. Section 351, however, can be invoked to, set at naught an order obtained from a court by practising fraud, by misleading it and where it passes an order or a decree upon misapprehension of the facts. I hold that such willful concealment on the part of the petitioners is a sufficient ground to invoke the provision of section 151 of the Code to set at naught the ex parte decree. 

 10. Now let me consider the contention that the application under Order 9 rule 13 read with Section 151 of Code admittedly being barred by limitation and there being no application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act the Court below ought not be have condoned the delay and passed the impugned order. According to article 164 of the Limitation Ad the period of limitation for setting aside a decree passed ex parte is thirty days from the date. of decree or where summons was not duly served, thirty days from the date of knowledge of the decree. Prior to 18.5.1967 Section 5 of the Limitation Act was not applicable to a proceeding under Order 9 rule 13. But by amendment made on 18.5.1967 Section 5 has been made applicable to such proceeding. In this respect the case of Khorshed Ali Chowdhury Vs. The People's Republic of Bangladesh, 29 DLR 376 may be referred to. In the instant case no separte application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act was filed along with the application under Order 9 rule 13 read with Section 151 of the Code. Therefore, the question that falls for determination is : Where no application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act is filed whether the Court is competent to set aside an ex parte decree merely on the basis of an application under Order 9 rule 13 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure? From a close reading of Section 5, it seems to me, that the court can condone the delay without such application provided the parties seeking relief satisfy the court that there was sufficient cause for not filing the application within time. Whether there was sufficient cause or not has to be gathered by the Court itself before whom such application is made from materials on record. In this case the reasons for delay have been duly stated by the opposite-parties in their application for setting aside the ex parte decree and in support of their case witnesses were also examined and evidences were led. From reading of the language of Section 5 of the Limitation Act I do not find that it enjoins upon a party filing an application under Order 9, rule 13 read with Section 151 of the Code to file a formal application under Section 5 of the said Act. In this case the panics having had duly stated the reasons for delay and as both the parties having had led evidence in support of their respective cases there could be no better or other reasons which could be stated in an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act and as such a formal application under Section 5 was not a must. It is also evident from record that there was no notice given by the court at Bashkhali to the opposite parties No. 1-3 regarding arrival of the records of the suit from Satkania which on transfer was re-numbered as partition suit No. 560 of 1984. In that event how can it be possible for them to know that the suit filed in the court of Munsif, Satkania was re-numbered as partition suit No. 560 of 1984 of the Court of Banshkhali without such notice from the Court? Taking this aspect into consideration, I am constrained to hold that there was sufficient cause for the opposite parties for not appearing at the time when the suit was called on for hearing and the delay in filing the application was sufficiently explained. The word" sufficient" cause should be construed liberally in order to advance the cause of substantial justice and not to shut out a litigant from the door of justice. A doctrinaire approach should be avoided because the court is to construe a provision of law for advancement of justice and not to retard it. A litigant should not- be deprived of the benefit to which he is otherwise entitled in law. As the court below found sufficient cause on consideration of the materials placed before it, it passed the impugned order., In the case of Mr. Kulsoomun Nissa and another Vs. Noor Mohammad alias Sultan Haider and another 1936 All 666, the learned Chief justice expressed himself in the following manner: 

 11. In the case of Firm Kaura Mal Vs. Firm Mathra Dass the Punjab High Court, 1959 Punj. 648 following 1930 All.  666 observed: Merely because there was no written application filed by the appellant was hardly sufficient ground for refusing him the relief, if he was otherwise entitled to it. 

 12. The view taken by their Lordships in the above cases has also been followed by our High Court Division in the case of Chowdhury Saifuddin Ahmed Vs. Sharnsuddin and others, 40 D.L.R., 10. That is a case directly on the point before me as there was not an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act. The trial Court dismissed the application filed for setting aside the ex parte decree on the ground that no application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act was filed for condo nation of delay. His Lordship Mustafa Kamal, J. following the decisions in the cases of Ms. Kulsoomun Nissa and Firm Kaura Mal observed: 

 "though as matter of prudence and Procedure a separate application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act is always desirable, no harm has been done in the present case as in the main application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure the appellant has sought to explain the reasons of his delay in filing the miscellaneous case". 

 13. Being in respectful agreement with his Lordship I hold that mere absence of a formal application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act in the present case is no bar to the grant of the relief sought for by an application under Order 9 rule 13 read with section 151 of the Code where in the said application all the facts constituting the delay are duly stated which are required to be stated in an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act on consideration of which the court is able to condone the delay. 

 14. Mr. N.I. Chowdhury, submitted further that the petitioners Nos. 18-24 who got saham should have been made opposite parties in the application and non-impleading them was defect of parties. He relied upon the decision in the case of Apil and other Vs. Ayatullah Pramanik and others, 6 D.L.R.  461. According to Order 9, rule 14 no decree shall be set aside unless notice of the application for setting aside the decree is served upon the opposite parties. In this case notices were served upon the plaintiffs and there was substantial compliance with the requirement of Order 9, rule 14 of the Code. On the other hand on the strength of Apil Bibi I hold that the plaintiffs- petitioners who got the ex parte decree are the opposite-parties within the meaning of Order 9 rule 14 of the Code as in the said decision it has been held that the plaintiffs in partition suit arc the opposite-panics within the meaning of Order 9 rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Therefore the decision does not help the learned Advocate. It is also urged that the Miscellaneous Case not having been decided in presence of petitioners Nos. 18-24 they have suffered loss. I do not find force in the contention. The suit being restored, in my opinion, they arc not to be debared from claiming the saham given and restoration of the suit does not prejudice them. It appears that the plea of defect of parties was taken in the written objection but no issue was framed on it by the trial Court nor the petitioners did press for framing the issue on the defect of parties. The petitioners also did not raise this point before the lower appellate Court. 

 15. Objection as to defect of parties has to be taken at the earliest time and after framing issues it should not be entertained. If not so taken, it shall be deemed to have been waived. In that view of the matter I hold that the petitioners also by their conduct waived the plea of defect of parties. The aforesaid view finds support from the decisions in the cases of Gurucharan Jena Vs. Satya Narayan Jew Thakur and others, 1971 Ori. 15; Parameswaran Vs. Shangaran, 14 Mad. 489. Vithabal vs. Pandu, 26 Born. 301., Khirsingti Vs. Brijlal 1949 Nag. 314 and in the case of Chandra Kanta Goswami Vs. Ram Nohiqi Debi and others 1956 Cal. 577. Therefore, the contention that the Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 1984 suffers from defect of parties has no force and cannot be allowed at this stage. 

 16. In this respect it is pertinent to observe that while granting an application for restoration of a suit on setting aside an ex parte decree the court is to allow the application upon such terms as to cost. As no cost has been awarded by the lower appellate court in this case, I direct the opposite-parties Nos. 1-3 to pay cost of Tk. 250/- to the petitioners. The court of Munsif, Bashkhali is also directed to communicate to the parties concerned about the transfer of the suit to that court and fix a date for hearing of the suit.
